questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: separate three words that share one English gloss by their register and topic
questions.stem: A learner is choosing between three Chinese words that all translate as to talk, and wants to know which one a speaker would use for a friendly chat with a friend over tea rather than for a work report. Which word is the chat one?

options.text: The word for chatting, since a friendly exchange has no agenda to discuss
The word for discussing, since any exchange of views counts as a discussion
options.misconception: treats a casual conversation as though it were a formal discussion

options.text: The word for speaking, since the general verb is always preferred in speech
options.misconception: assumes the general verb is the natural choice in informal conversation

options.text: All three are interchangeable, and the choice between them is only regional
options.misconception: believes register differences in a word set are only matters of place

questions.explanation: The three words divide the work by what the talk is for. The general verb covers simply speaking, and it is what you use when nothing more needs saying. The word for discussing carries a subject matter and a slightly official air, so it turns up in meetings, in the phrase for talking about work, and in reports. The word used in the compound for chatting is reserved for talk whose point is the company rather than the content, which is why it takes a social object instead of a topic. The temptation is to treat all three as synonyms because English uses one short word for the whole range.
questions.hint: Ask whether the talk has a subject matter, or whether the company is the point.

questions.learningObjective: sort four time words by the stretch of time each one names
questions.stem: A writer needs two different words, one for a stretch of decades within a century and one for time as a general measurable thing. Which pair does the language actually use?

options.text: The word for decades, and the word for time in general as a measurable thing
The word for time in general, and the word for decades of a century
options.misconception: swaps the two while keeping the idea that they name different stretches

options.text: The word for an occasion, and the word for an era of history as a whole
options.misconception: picks an occasion word and an era word instead of the right pair

options.text: The word for an era, and the word for an occasion or a point in time
options.misconception: chooses the two coarsest time words rather than the two wanted

questions.explanation: Four related words are in play and each has its own scale. The word for an occasion names a point or a stretch inside a day, as in at that time. The word for time names the general thing you can spend or lose. The word for decades names a numbered stretch inside a century, so the nineteen-eighties and the nineteen-nineties each take it. The word for an era names a large historical stretch, such as an age of thought or an age of expansion, and it usually carries a judgement. A learner who reaches for the era word when the meaning is a numbered decade has overshot by a whole register.
questions.hint: Ask how wide the stretch of time is, and whether a century can be divided by it.

The given name comes first, and the family name is written at the very end
options.misconception: puts the family name last, the way an English name is arranged

options.text: The family name comes last, and the first character is always the given name
options.misconception: reverses the order while sounding as though it were decided

options.text: Both halves are given names, and one of them is a courtesy name used in writing
options.misconception: invents a third name function to avoid admitting a family name

questions.stem: An English speaker has to say that a woman has a brother who is older than her, and one English word will not do the job. Why does the language need two words?

questions.learningObjective: explain the precision of the set of words for the English word uncle

questions.learningObjective: explain why one word names both a grandmother and a much younger stepmother
questions.stem: A single word is used in one family both for a man's father's mother and for a young woman married to his father's father. Which word serves both, and why?

The word for a mother, shared by a man's own mother and by his father's wife
options.misconception: moves the ambiguity onto the two women who are a generation apart

options.text: The word for an aunt, used for any older woman living inside one household
options.misconception: widens the word to a whole category of women in a home

questions.learningObjective: identify the extra information carried by the two words for a brother's wife

options.text: How far away the cousin lives, since one word means a cousin living abroad
options.misconception: reads a difference of family line as though it were about geography

questions.learningObjective: explain a change in a word's meaning between an older text and present speech
questions.stem: In older writing the word now used for going along on foot could also mean to run, and an old phrase about riding a horse at a gallop still contains it. What does that show about the word?

options.text: Its meaning has narrowed over time, so a modern gloss hides what it once meant
It has two separate meanings today, and the older one has not gone anywhere
options.misconception: believes both the old and the new senses are available in speech now

options.text: It always covered both, and the difference is only in how formal the tone is
options.misconception: turns a change of meaning into a difference of politeness

options.text: The older meaning belonged to a different word written with the same character
options.misconception: escapes the evidence by claiming the old writer meant a different word

The reason a learner meets the old meaning in a text is that the older sense is preserved in the writing even after the speech has moved on.

questions.learningObjective: state the effect the light child-suffix has on a spoken word
questions.stem: A speaker pronounces the word for a small child and the word for smell with a light extra syllable that a textbook does not print, and both sound warmer and more familiar. What is that suffix doing?

options.text: It softens the word and makes it familiar, and sometimes makes it smaller
It makes the word more formal, because the extra sound marks respect for the topic
options.misconception: reads a spoken softening as though it added formality or respect

options.text: It turns the word into a plural, since the extra sound marks more than one thing
options.misconception: treats the extra syllable as a number marker rather than a softener

options.text: It restores an older reading, so the suffixed form is the more literary one
options.misconception: believes the extra syllable returns a word to an archaic sense

questions.explanation: This suffix is a vowel added to the end of a syllable, and it does two things that learners often expect to be separate. It very often makes a word sound small, affectionate or casual, which is why it turns up on the word for a child and on the word for smell and on the word for a little thing. And it also just loosens the register, so a great many words carry it with no sense of smallness at all, and speakers use it by habit. It is also largely a feature of speech rather than of writing, and it is more common in the north, so a learner who meets it everywhere in a novel and nowhere in a textbook has met one register rather than the language.
questions.hint: Ask how the speaker would sound if the extra syllable were left off in each case.

questions.learningObjective: exclude the two words where the light suffix is not a diminutive at all

options.misconception: names the clearest examples of the suffix as though they were the exceptions

options.misconception: confuses the diminutive suffix with the two words that compare ages

options.misconception: claims the suffix is a particle in a set of ordinary time expressions

questions.learningObjective: classify the shared ending of a set of place and object nouns
questions.stem: A learner sees that the words for stone, bone, steamed bun and a piece of wood all end in the same short unstressed syllable. What kind of element is that shared ending?

options.text: A suffix that builds a family of concrete nouns, read in the neutral tone
A full second syllable of each word, carrying its own tone in every case
options.misconception: misses that the ending carries no tone of its own anywhere in the set

options.text: A classifier that must move to the front of the phrase before these nouns
options.misconception: confuses a word-forming suffix with the classifier that counts the noun

options.text: A single word borrowed whole and added to four separate native roots
options.misconception: invents a loan to explain a productive native pattern

It is always short and light, which is why a learner who expects a tone mark on it never finds one, and a speaker who gives it a full tone sounds odd. The suffix is productive, so a learner who knows it can often guess the meaning of an unfamiliar word that contains it, which is a real shortcut. The trap is that a few common words merely start with the same two characters, most obviously the word for hair, where the second part is an ordinary full-tone syllable and not the suffix at all.

questions.learningObjective: accept that the set of nouns taking a common suffix has to be learned rather than predicted
questions.stem: A learner collects six nouns that end in the same short unstressed syllable, notices that several similar-looking nouns do not, and asks for a rule. What is the honest answer?

options.text: The ending is a matter of which roots habitually take it, so the set must be learned
Every made object takes the ending, and no natural thing ever takes it
options.misconception: believes a made-versus-natural rule predicts the whole set

options.text: The ending is added whenever the noun is longer than one syllable in writing
options.misconception: thinks word length in characters decides which nouns take the ending

options.text: The ending marks plurals, so a noun carrying it means more than one of the thing
options.misconception: reads a noun-forming suffix as though it were a plural marker

The words for table, chair, plate, bottle, hat and cup all take it, while the words for fish, cat, book and apple do not, and nothing about made objects or word length predicts which group a word falls into. questions.learningObjective: state what repeating a two-syllable adjective does to its strength
questions.stem: A speaker says a four-syllable form of clean about a table, and a learner expects a mild word meaning simply clean. What has the repetition done to the meaning?

options.text: It has strengthened the word, so the table is spotless rather than only clean
It has weakened the word, so the table is only fairly clean after all
options.misconception: assumes repetition always softens, which is true of verbs and not adjectives

options.text: It has turned the word into a plural, naming several clean tables at once
options.misconception: reads an intensified adjective as though it were a number marker

options.text: It has marked the sentence as a question about whether the table is clean
options.misconception: believes a reduplicated adjective signals doubt about a claim

questions.explanation: Repeating a two-syllable adjective strengthens it to mean entirely so, so the four-syllable form about the table says the table is spotless, with no trace of dirt anywhere. The same pattern gives a cheerful form for happy and a smooth form for smooth, and a native speaker uses them freely. The four-syllable version is the one that appears in writing, while the shortened two-syllable version is what most people actually say, and the two mean the same thing. questions.learningObjective: separate the softening effect of a repeated verb from a second action
questions.stem: A speaker says the repeated form of look and the repeated form of think where a textbook would print the plain verbs, and a learner wonders whether two separate actions are meant. What does the repetition contribute?

options.text: It makes the action brief and casual, softening the request rather than adding meaning
It adds a second action, so the speaker is really asking for two things to be done
options.misconception: takes a repeated verb as two separate events rather than one softened one

options.text: It marks the action as finished, so the looking is now completely in the past
options.misconception: reads the second syllable as a completion marker rather than part of the verb

options.text: It makes the action polite and formal, as though a stranger were being asked
options.misconception: believes a casual softening makes a request more formal and not less

The pattern is so productive that almost any verb can be repeated this way, and adding the word for a while beforehand softens it further, so the effect is available at three strengths rather than one.

questions.learningObjective: recognise that a repeated noun means every one of its members
questions.stem: A speaker uses a repeated word for person and a repeated word for day in a sentence about a community, and a learner takes both for ordinary plurals. What are the two forms actually doing?

options.text: Each one means every single member, spreading the word across the whole group
Each one is a polite plural, and the plain word would sound far too familiar
options.misconception: reads a distributive meaning as though it were a matter of politeness

options.text: Each one marks a rough number, so the speaker cannot be exact about how many
options.misconception: believes repetition signals vagueness rather than universality

options.text: Each one is a formal written form that spoken language always shortens
options.misconception: claims the spoken form is the shortened one and both are written

There is a neighbouring pattern worth knowing, where the word for one is put in front twice instead, and that one means one at a time, so a learner who mixes the two patterns will say that things were done one at a time when the meaning was every one of them.
questions.hint: Ask whether the form allows exceptions and whether it gives a number at all.

questions.learningObjective: resolve an ambiguous short form from the surrounding context
questions.stem: A speaker says the same two-character short form twice in one morning, once about a university and once about a national body, and a learner is sure it is one thing. What settles it?

options.misconception: invents two different written forms for what is one short form

options.text: The age of the speaker, because only younger people use it for the university
options.misconception: believes usage is split by generation rather than by context

A difference in register, where one word is formal and the other is slang

A difference in politeness, with the northern sense being the more casual of the two

questions.learningObjective: identify a festival from its three best-known customs
questions.stem: A family describes what they did on the first evening of the year, and the list includes a set meal, red packets containing money, and staying up late. Which festival is this, and what are those three things?

options.text: The spring festival, whose customs are a reunion dinner, money gifts, and staying up
The lantern festival, whose customs are a reunion dinner, money gifts, and staying up
options.misconception: gives the spring festival's customs to the lantern festival

options.text: The mid-autumn festival, whose customs are round pastries, lanterns, and a night outing

options.text: The dragon boat festival, whose customs are a reunion dinner, boat races, and dumplings

questions.learningObjective: state what a summary must keep and what it may leave out

answer.exemplar: A summary has to keep the claim and drop the evidence, and the mistake in the learner's sentence is almost certainly that it dropped one of the claims instead of some of the support for a claim. Start by asking what the original is for. If four sentences about a community garden are there to report an outcome, the outcome is the claim: the plot was cleared and turned into beds, fewer people came than had signed up, and the harvest was shared in August. That outcome is what a one-sentence version must still say, including the part that went badly, because dropping the disappointing number does not make the summary tidier, it makes it untrue. A summary is allowed to leave out the individual names, the dates of each work day, the price of the timber and the arguments about where to put the water butt, because none of those is what the passage concludes. It is also allowed to compress a list into a category, so a paragraph that names six vegetables becomes a sentence that says home-grown vegetables. What it is not allowed to do is settle a dispute the original left open, sharpen a tendency into a fact, or add a reason the original never gave, and those three additions are what a learner most often makes by accident when shortening a passage, because joining things up is easier than leaving them loose. A good check is to put the original and the summary side by side and ask whether a reader who had seen only the summary would be misled about anything. If the answer is no, the sentence is short enough and the claim has survived.

Learners who can shorten a passage usually cannot yet say why one shortening works and another does not, and the reason is that they are thinking about length rather than about claim. Framing the work as claim versus evidence makes the two halves of the task separable: the claim must survive, the evidence is free to go. Naming the three additions that summaries most often smuggle in, a settled dispute, a sharpened tendency, an invented reason, is worth the time it takes, because those are the failures that survive a careful reading and turn up later as a misreading of the source.
questions.hint: Ask what the original four sentences were for, and which of their words a reader would need in order to know that.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: choose a register for a translation and then rewrite in it
questions.stem: Stage one: a message to a customer says the order was posted yesterday and should arrive within three working days, and a translator must decide how formal the Chinese should sound for a first-time business contact. Say what that choice is. Stage two: write the sentence in the register you chose, keeping both facts exactly as they were given.

answer.exemplar: Stage one: the choice is a polite, written register, the one a business uses with somebody it does not know yet. The deciding facts are all in the situation rather than in the words. A first-time contact means the relationship has not been established, so the marker of respect has to be there; a customer means the sender is the one who wants something, so the message cannot sound like a note between equals; and two hard facts, a posting date and a delivery window, mean the sentence is transactional and the politeness has to be carried by the wording around the facts rather than by the facts themselves. A learner who answers casual here has picked the register of a friend rather than the register of a supplier, and the message will read as either rude or careless, depending on how much the recipient likes being a customer. Stage two: one sentence that keeps both facts and holds the register is 您好，您的订单已于昨日寄出，预计三个工作日内送达。 The posted date is in the middle, stated as a completed fact; the window follows as an estimate, with the expected word marking it as a promise about a range rather than a guarantee; and the opening word marks the respect before any content arrives. A version that keeps the same two facts but reads like a text message to a friend drops the respect marker and shortens the window, and a version that keeps the respect marker but adds an apology the original never contained has translated the relationship as well as the message, which is a different mistake. The check that catches both is to read the sentence twice, once as the sender and once as the customer, and ask whether each reading finds anything the other did not put there.

questions.explanation: The two stages test different things and the pairing is the point. Choosing a register is a judgement about a relationship, and a learner can usually do it if asked directly. Writing in that register is a production task that exposes every gap in the judgement, because the words available in the chosen register do not line up one for one with the words in the source, and a learner who has only ever named registers will freeze at that point. The pairing also keeps the content honest, since both stages insist on the same two facts, so a fluent rewrite cannot be rewarded for quietly dropping the delivery window, which is the most common way a learner improves a sentence without improving the message.
questions.hint: Ask who wrote the message, who reads it, and whether the two have spoken before, then build the sentence around the two facts.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: state a cultural claim so that a reader could check it
questions.stem: A student wants to write a short note about how tea is served when a guest arrives, and an instructor insists that every cultural claim must be stated so that a reader could go and check it. Which version of the claim satisfies that?

options.text: In many households tea is offered to a guest soon after they arrive
Tea has always been the most respected drink in every part of the world
options.misconception: makes a worldwide ranking claim that no reader could check

options.text: Chinese people are politer about tea than anyone else in any situation
options.misconception: turns one practice into a national superiority claim about politeness

options.text: Tea drinking in China is so old that nobody can say when it began
options.misconception: hides an untestable claim about origins behind a vague statement of great age

questions.explanation: A checkable claim is one that names who does what, and it can be marked right or wrong by somebody who goes and looks. The accepted version does that: it says that in many households a guest is offered tea soon after arriving, which a reader can confirm or contradict by spending an afternoon in a few of them. The scope word matters as much as the content, since a claim limited to many households is honest about its own reach, while a claim about everyone is false the first time one counterexample appears. Option B reaches outside the culture being described and ranks drinks across the world, which no single reader could verify at all. Option C is the commonest failure in student writing about culture, because it turns a specific courtesy into a national character and then compares that character with other nations. Option D is subtler and worth naming, since it sounds like modesty about deep history, but it makes a factual claim about origins and then declares it unavailable.
questions.hint: Ask what a reader would have to observe, and how many, in order to be able to agree or disagree with the sentence.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: rewrite an absolute cultural claim into one that can be checked
questions.stem: A visitor's report says that in this country a gift should always be handed over with both hands, and a reviewer rewrites the sentence so that somebody could go and check it. Which rewrite is the checkable one?

options.text: Holding an offered item with both hands is used as a sign of respect
Nobody in this country has ever handed anything over with one hand
options.misconception: states an absolute that a single counterexample would disprove

options.text: Everyone here insists that both hands are the correct choice for any gift
options.misconception: keeps the original absolutes and only softens the phrasing

options.text: Both hands are used in this country for every kind of exchange whatever its meaning
options.misconception: extends the practice to exchanges that nobody would class as gifts

questions.explanation: The original sentence hides two absolutes, in always and in should, and both have to go before the sentence can be checked. The accepted rewrite replaces them with a claim about what a practice is used to signal, which is observable: you can watch a handover, and you can see whether the visitor is being treated with more care than an ordinary one. A claim of that shape is also the one a reader can correct, because a counterexample is easy to describe. The rejected versions all sound like small repairs, which is exactly why they are instructive. Option B and option C each keep one absolute and swap the other for a vague intensifier, so nothing about them can be confirmed. Option D widens the practice from gift-giving to every exchange whatever its meaning, which is a claim about paying a shopkeeper and settling an argument, and no observer would accept it.
questions.hint: Find the words in the original sentence that cannot be true, and check whether each rewrite still contains one of them.

questions.subject: CHINESE
questions.learningObjective: accept only the joins between two clauses that a speaker would use
questions.stem: A writer tests five ways of joining two short Chinese clauses into a single sentence, and a speaker would say three of them without changing a word. Which three are those?

options.text: 菜很便宜，味道也不错。
他不但会说中文，还会写毛笔字。
因为下雨了，所以我们改在天桥见面。
options.misconception: marks a cause word and a result word as though both were required in one sentence

options.text: 他非常努力，因此成绩进步得很快。
他虽然努力了，因此成绩进步很快。
options.misconception: expects a clause opening with a concession to lead straight into a result

questions.explanation: The test is not whether a join is understandable but whether a speaker would produce it, and the two rejected versions are understandable enough to be the interesting cases. The first accepted sentence needs no connective at all, because the second clause marks itself as additional with a word that already means also. The second accepted sentence uses the paired form that opens a concession of scope and closes it with an addition, so the reader knows that the first thing said is not the only thing said. The third accepted sentence takes one connective and one half of the causal pair, which is what a speaker does when the link is obvious. The first rejected sentence marks both halves of the causal pair in the same sentence, and that is the mark of a translation rather than a speaker, because the reason is already there and the result word says nothing extra. The second rejected sentence opens a concession and never closes it, then runs straight into a result, so the reader is left holding a turn that was never taken.
questions.hint: Read each sentence as something a person would actually say on the telephone, and ask whether the connectives are doing two jobs where one is enough.
